title: Meeting Rooms
statement: One person has a list of meetings, each with a start time and an end time. Decide whether they can attend all of them, which means no two meetings overlap in time. A meeting that starts exactly when another one ends does not clash with it. Return true or false.

example.caption: [3,5] and [4,6] overlap between 4 and 5, so the answer is false.

idea.sentence: Sort the meetings by start time. If any two overlap, some neighbouring pair in that order overlaps, so only neighbours need checking.

jargon.plain: Two meetings clash when the later one starts strictly before the earlier one ends. Equal times do not clash.
Two meetings next to each other after sorting by start.

watch.inputHint: One argument: a list of [start, end] pairs, e.g. [[6,7],[1,2],[2,3],[3,5],[4,6]]

rows.name: Compare all pairs
rows.note: Check each pair for overlap. Simple, but slow for long lists.

rows.name: Sort, then neighbours
rows.note: The sort dominates. The copy costs O(n) space; sorting in place would not, but it edits the input.

fast.takeaway: Sorting by start puts every possible clash next to each other, so one linear pass is enough.

stages.title: Sort by start
stages.note: Sort a copy by start with a numeric comparator.

stages.title: Compare neighbours
stages.note: Does this meeting start before the previous one ends? Strictly before: equal is fine.

stages.title: Verdict
stages.note: A clash returns false at once. If the loop finishes with none, return true.

edges.title: Back to back
edges.why: Each meeting starts at the exact time the last one ends. The test is start < end, so these do not clash.

edges.title: Empty schedule
edges.why: No meetings, nothing to attend, nothing to clash. The loop never runs.

edges.title: One inside another
edges.why: [3,4] starts before [1,10] ends. Only the start of the later one matters for this test.

edges.title: Same slot twice
edges.why: Identical meetings overlap fully. 4 < 6, so the pair is a clash.

gotchas.text: Touching is not a clash here: use start < prevEnd. Merge Intervals uses <= because it wants touching intervals joined. Same shape, opposite rule.
intervals.sort() with no comparator sorts as strings, so [10,11] lands before [2,3]. Pass (a, b) => a[0] - b[0].
sort() edits the array in place, so the caller's list would end up reordered. Sort a copy: [...intervals].
sort.Slice reorders the slice you give it, and the caller shares that memory. Copy first with append([][]int(nil), intervals...).

recap.key: After sorting by start, a clash exists exactly when some meeting starts before the previous one ends.
recap.complexity: Time O(n log n). Space O(n).
moves: Sort a copy by start (numeric comparator)
For each neighbouring pair, test next.start < prev.end
Return false on the first clash
